title: The Peasant and the Bear

sources.author: Valery Carrick, translated by Nevill Forbes
sources.title: More Russian Picture Tales

provenance.rights: The text is our own retelling of a traditional Russian folk tale, written for Omramo; it does not use the wording of the cited edition. The cited edition is in the US public domain (published before 1931); other territories not verified. Legal review pending (PRD Q23).

geography.lesson: Russia's great forests and the farm fields at their edge; summers in the north are short, so villagers grew root crops such as turnips, and grain such as rye.

culture.lesson: Village farming in old Russia (plough, sickle, turnips, rye and black bread), and the bear as the best-known animal of Russian tales: big, blustery and easily outwitted.

moral.lesson: Think before you agree to a bargain. The hasty Bear chooses twice without asking what is being planted; the careful Peasant knows that tops or roots depends on the crop.
moral.reflectionQuestion: What should the Bear have asked before he said “Done!”?

moral: Think and ask before you agree to a bargain.

cover.alt: A peasant holding up a round turnip and a big brown bear holding a bunch of green leaves, side by side in a field.

card.label: Character · in Part I and Part II
card.title: The Peasant
card.body: He has one field, one horse and one wooden plough. He knows what grows up and what grows down. When a bear roars at him, he takes off his cap and makes a plan.
card.portraitAlt: The Peasant in a red shirt and a cap, holding a round turnip by its leaves.

card.label: Character · in Part I and Part II
card.title: The Bear
card.body: He says the forest is his, and he roars a great deal. But he would much rather eat than fight. He says “Done!” before he has asked a single question.
card.portraitAlt: The big brown Bear sitting down, chewing a green turnip leaf and looking puzzled.

paras: ^At the edge of a great <tap:forest>forest</tap> lived a poor <name:peasant>Peasant</name>.
A peasant is a farmer who owns very little. This one had one field, one horse and one wooden plough.
One spring morning he went out to plough. The earth turned over, dark and soft, and the birds sang in the birch trees.
<pop:1.3>Crack!</pop> went the bushes. Out of the forest came a great brown <name:bear>Bear</name>.
<say:bear*>“Peasant!”</say> he roared. <say:bear>“This is my forest. I will break you up like a stick!”</say>
The horse stopped. The birds stopped. But the Peasant did not run. He took off his cap.
<say:peasant*>“Don’t, Bear,”</say> he said. <say:peasant>“Let us share. I will do the sowing. When the crop is ripe, you take the tops, and I will take only the roots.”</say>
The Bear scratched his ear. Tops were on top. Tops must be best.
He did not ask what the Peasant was sowing. <say:bear*>“Done!”</say> he said, and he ambled back into the trees.
Summer is short in the north, so the Peasant did not waste a day.
He sowed. He weeded. He chased away the crows.
Up came the leaves, thick and green. Now and then the Bear came by to look.
<say:bear*>“My tops are growing nicely,”</say> he said.
Autumn came. The birch leaves turned yellow, and the Bear came for his share.
The Peasant took hold of some leaves and pulled. <pop:1.3>Pop!</pop> Out of the dark earth came a <tap:turnip>turnip</tap>, fat and white. Then another, and another.
He cut off the green tops and made a heap. <say:peasant*>“Yours, Bear. Just as we agreed.”</say>
The Bear sat down by his heap of leaves. He chewed one. It was tough. It was bitter.
The Peasant loaded his cart. In went the turnips, round as <tap:saint-basils-moment>onions</tap>, until the cart was full.
The Bear stopped chewing. <say:bear*>“What have you got there, Peasant?”</say>
<say:peasant*>“Only my roots, Bear. I am taking them to town to sell.”</say>
<say:bear*>“Give me one to try.”</say>
The Peasant tossed him a turnip, and the Bear bit it in two. <pop:1.3>Crunch!</pop>
It was sweet. It was juicy. It was much, much nicer than leaves.
<say:bear*>“Grrr!”</say> said the Bear. <say:bear>“Your roots are sweet and my tops are bitter. Next year, I take the roots!”</say>
<say:peasant*>“As you wish, Bear,”</say> said the Peasant. <say:peasant>“Next year the roots are yours, and I will take only the tops.”</say>
The Bear nodded hard. Once again, he did not ask what would be sown.
^Next spring the Peasant ploughed his field again.
His <name:wife>wife</name> carried out a sack of seed. <say:wife*>“Turnips again?”</say> she asked.
<say:peasant*>“Not this year,”</say> said the Peasant. <say:peasant>“This year we sow <tap:rye>rye</tap>.”</say> And he scattered the grain by the handful, left and right.
Far off in the trees, the Bear rubbed his paws. <say:bear*>“My roots,”</say> he said. <say:bear>“My sweet, sweet roots.”</say>
The rye came up green. All summer it grew, up to the Peasant’s knee, up to his belt, up to his shoulder.
Then it turned gold, and it whispered when the wind blew.
Every day the Bear came to look. <say:bear*>“Grow, roots, grow,”</say> he sang. He never once looked at the tops.
At harvest time the Peasant came with his sickle, a knife curved like a new moon.
Swish, swish, swish! Down fell the golden rye. His wife tied it into sheaves, and they stacked the sheaves on the cart.
<say:peasant*>“Now, Bear,”</say> said the Peasant, <say:peasant>“the roots are yours. Every one.”</say>
The Bear dug. He pulled up a root, thin and dry as string. He chewed it. He pulled a face.
<say:bear*>“Peasant!”</say> he roared. <say:bear>“Tops, and I get leaves. Roots, and I get string! How do you do it?”</say>
<say:peasant*>“I don’t do it, Bear. The crop does. Turnips grow down. Rye grows up. You never asked what I was sowing.”</say>
The Bear sat on his heap of roots and thought for a long time.
In the village, the Peasant’s wife baked black bread from the new rye. The whole house smelled of it.
Before the first snow, the Peasant carried a warm loaf and a basket of turnips to the edge of the forest. He left them on a stump.
The Bear found them. He ate the loaf. He ate the turnips. He licked the basket.
<say:bear*>“Next spring,”</say> he said, with his mouth full, <say:bear>“I will not say tops, and I will not say roots. I will say: Peasant, what are we planting?”</say>
Then he yawned a great yawn, and went off to sleep until spring.

landmarks.name: Saint Basil’s Cathedral

low.line: Its bright roofs are shaped like onions. No two are the same.

medium.line: It was built on Red Square in Moscow more than 450 years ago, for a ruler named Ivan.
medium.note: Roofs with this shape are called onion domes. Each one has its own colours and pattern.

advanced.line: Built from 1555 to 1561 for Tsar Ivan IV, it stands on Red Square with a cluster of onion domes around one tall central tower.
advanced.note: Old records name its builders as Barma and Postnik, but no one is sure who they were. The bright colours were added later.

art.alt: A cluster of towers topped with bright onion-shaped domes, striped and patterned in red, green, blue, gold and white, around one tall pointed tower.

landmarks.rights: Our own illustration; no photograph. A religious building, presented as architecture and history only (CONTENT_PLAN §5, CQ9). Landmark image rights review pending (PRD Q29).

sourceNotes: This is our own retelling, written for Omramo, of a traditional Russian village folk tale
(the “tops and roots” tale of a farmer and a bear who share a crop). It is not the wording of any earlier edition.
Documented source for the tale: Valery Carrick, “More Russian Picture Tales”, translated by Nevill Forbes (1914),
Project Gutenberg ebook #23462, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/23462 (US public domain; other territories not verified).
The book is verified; the tale’s printed title in that book was not confirmed. Project Gutenberg could not be reached
when this text was written, so it was written from the traditional shape of the tale, not from the cited pages.
Softened: the Bear’s threat is kept short and comic. Older tellings end with the two as enemies, and some go on to a
hunt; both are left out. Our ending (the gift of bread and turnips, the Bear’s new question) is our own addition.
To check: rye is sown in spring here, as the tale needs; much Russian rye was sown in autumn. Russian reader to confirm.
Status: DRAFT. Text review pending. Cultural review (standard: Russian reader) pending.
Source check, 18 Nov 2026 (read on the Project Gutenberg mirror gutenberg.pglaf.org; gutenberg.org itself was unreachable):
The tale is in Carrick's book, printed as “The Peasant and the Bear” (the fourth of ten tales; Frederick A. Stokes Company, New York; the Gutenberg text is a 1920 printing of the 1914 book).

Carrick's version differs from ours: his peasant is a widower who invites the bear to farm with him, the bear works beside him, there is no threat, the second crop is wheat, the bear never tastes a turnip, and he leaves calling the peasant too crafty. Our telling follows the commonly told Russian form (the bear's threat, tops and roots), with rye for the second crop, a living wife and a warm ending; no second edition is cited for that form yet (open question for the Russian reader and for PRD Q23).

palette.mood: Fresh, open and friendly: pale northern sky, white birch trunks, dark earth, then turnip gold and rye gold; one red shirt as the bright note.

artBrief.light: Clear morning or late-afternoon daylight, never dusk; ONE warm light from the upper left in every picture, with soft long shadows falling to the right.
world: Central Russian countryside: flat or gently rolling land, a small strip field of dark soil right against the forest edge.
The forest is mixed: silver birch (white bark with black marks, light airy crowns) in front, dark pointed spruce and a few pines behind. Keep the tree line low enough that the sky above stays pale.
The plough is a light wooden plough (a sokha) pulled by ONE small, sturdy, shaggy farm horse with a wooden arch (a duga) over its collar. No tractor, no metal machinery, no heavy Western horse team.
The cart is a simple four-wheeled wooden farm cart (a telega) with low sides. Turnips are the old northern kind: round and slightly flat, pale yellow-white with a leafy green top, the size of a fist.
Rye stands shoulder-high, with long bearded ears that nod over; it is reaped with a hand sickle and tied into sheaves stood up in small stacks.

The house in the distance is a log house (an izba): round logs, a steep plank or thatch roof, small windows with simple carved frames, a well with a long pole. The village is a few such houses and a plain wooden fence.
Seasons must read clearly: spring (bare dark earth, fresh small birch leaves), autumn (yellow birch leaves, low gold light), high summer (blue sky, tall gold rye), harvest (stubble, sheaves, sacks).
The bear is a Eurasian brown bear: round, heavy, shaggy, with small round ears. Comic and expressive, never snarling; no bared teeth or claws aimed at anyone.

AVOID: fur hats and snow in summer scenes, balalaikas, nesting dolls, vodka, onion-domed churches in the scene art (the landmark appears only on its card), a bear in clothes or on a chain, a circus bear, ragged ‘misery’ poverty.
AVOID religious imagery in the scenes (no icons or crosses needed), and any modern object.

characters.peasant: A wiry, cheerful man of middle years with a short brown beard and a sun-browned face. A long red belted shirt with a side-fastened collar, loose striped trousers, cloth leg-wraps and woven bark shoes; a soft peaked cap that he takes off when he talks to the Bear. Calm eyes with a small smile.
characters.bear: A very large, round brown bear with a paler muzzle, small round ears and thick eyebrows that show every feeling: bluster, puzzlement, delight. He often sits upright like a person at a table. Signature detail: a turnip leaf or a rye stalk stuck in the corner of his mouth.
characters.wife: A sturdy, bright-eyed woman in a green sleeveless dress over a white blouse with a little red stitching at the cuffs, a plain headscarf tied at the back, an apron. She carries things: a seed sack, a sheaf, a loaf.

scene-field.unfolded: Far: a low band of pale blue-green forest and a wide pale spring sky. Middle: the birch-and-spruce forest edge rising on the trailing (right) half, kept below the top quarter. Near: across the bottom, furrows of dark earth; on the trailing half the Peasant with his wooden plough and small horse, and the Bear stepping out of the bushes towards them. The leading (left) pane's upper two thirds are calm pale sky for the words, with only a few small birds.
scene-field.folded: A tall band: pale sky above, the Bear's surprised-fierce face and shoulders in the middle between two white birch trunks, the Peasant (cap in hand) and the horse's head small at the bottom.

scene-turnips.unfolded: Far: yellow autumn birches and a pale sky with a few high clouds. Middle: the pulled field, rows of turnips lying on the soil. Near, on the trailing half: the wooden cart heaped with round turnips, the Peasant lifting one in; low across the centre, the Bear sitting beside his big heap of green leaves, one leaf in his mouth. The leading pane's upper two thirds stay pale sky; a few yellow leaves drift down.
scene-turnips.folded: The Bear's doubtful face in the middle, a turnip leaf hanging from his mouth, his heap of leaves below him and the turnip cart's wheel and load at one side; pale sky above.

scene-rye.unfolded: Far: a low blue line of forest under a high, pale summer sky. Middle and near: a sea of golden rye across both panes, filling the lower third only, its ears catching the light. On the trailing half the Bear stands at the field's edge, chest-deep in rye, watching it grow with his paws together. The leading pane's upper two thirds are calm sky; one or two swallows.
scene-rye.folded: Golden rye across the lower half, the Bear's hopeful face rising out of it in the middle, pale blue sky above.

scene-harvest.unfolded: Far, small and low on the leading half: a log house with a steep roof, a well pole and two or three more roofs of the village, with a thread of chimney smoke. Middle: stubble field with standing sheaves. Near, on the trailing half: the Peasant beside the cart stacked with golden sheaves and full sacks; low in the centre the Bear sitting on a heap of thin dry roots and stubble, holding one root up and frowning at it. The leading pane's upper two thirds stay pale late-summer sky.
scene-harvest.folded: The Bear's puzzled face in the middle, holding up a stringy root; behind him the cart of golden sheaves; a tiny log house on the horizon; pale sky above.

pictures.forest: One centred subject: the forest edge, three or four white birch trunks with light green leaves in front of dark pointed spruces, a strip of grass below. No people, no animals.
pictures.turnip: One centred subject: a single round, slightly flat turnip, pale yellow-white, with a tuft of fresh green leaves and a little dark soil still on its thin root tail.
pictures.rye: One centred subject: one sheaf of golden rye tied with a twist of straw, its bearded ears nodding at the top. No loaf, no people.

portraits.peasant: Head and shoulders to the waist, facing us with a small smile: red shirt, cap pushed back, holding a round turnip up by its leaves. Warm gold background.
portraits.bear: The Bear sitting upright, round and shaggy, a turnip leaf in the corner of his mouth and his eyebrows up in a puzzled look. Soft green background.

artBrief.cover: The Peasant and the Bear side by side in the middle of the field, seen from the front: the Peasant holds up a round turnip, the Bear holds up a bunch of green leaves and eyes the turnip. Birch trees behind, pale sky above for the title.

landmarks.saint-basils-cathedral: Our own drawing of the cathedral by day, seen from Red Square, centred: the cluster of towers with onion domes, each with its own stripes, swirls or diamond pattern in red, green, blue, gold and white, around the taller central tent-shaped tower; red brick walls with white trim. Presented as a building only: keep any crosses on the domes very small and plain, no people at worship, no flags or modern signs, a clear pale sky fading into the deep blue card colour below.
